description: I am a Cork-based engineering student focusing on systems and ergonomic design. For Astrolymics, we are building a reliable, low-cognitive-load health monitoring tool for astronauts on space missions. Join us if you want to deliver a functional, well-engineered prototype rather than just conceptual slides. Seeking teammates skilled in software development (full-stack/mobile), machine learning or telemetry data.
summary:
In space. All alone. No hospital. No professional help. Isolation. What would you do if you were in this scenario? Well, astronauts face these troubles daily, and oftentimes have to resort to neglecting their health completely. Hence we – a group of 6 dedicated students – have come together to conceptualise and design…


The Astrolympics.

With this, astronauts can monitor their health through a series of games, adding light to their lives while they’re drifting into an abyss. In each of the 6 modules, the crew can compete to climb to the top of the leaderboard, encouraging them to work as a team while also improving their health; not alone, but together. As a team.


So bring your crew along. Push your pace, own your space.
details:
Our project focuses on various submodules of health which need to be taken into account when travelling in space. Good health is vital for astronauts while on missions. During our research, we noticed that health can easily go unnoticed. And what did we do about this?

We conceptualised and partially prototyped a software that brings light to the crews’ – hypothetical – day. Through immersive experiences, we highlighted, assessed and explored the urgent need for health protocols for astronauts, while allowing them to have a balanced life and still enjoy the leisure of games.

Oftentimes, a person's wellbeing goes unnoticed, especially if they are in space, isolated from the rest of the population. Additionally, more often than not, this isolation can further lead to a deterioration in both their physical and mental states, affecting their ability to work efficiently.

An astronaut's health can be put at risk by various factors, including exposure to space radiation, altered gravity and a hostile, closed environment. So many factors can negatively affect an astronaut in an unimaginable number of ways, but only so much can be done to help. And that is why we have established the Astrolympics.

We used a multitude of components to piece the project together, including Visual Studio Code, IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate, Webflow and more. We collaborated using our unique individual skills in order to produce the project.

In terms of coding, we used Visual Studio Code to program the cognitive performance software (Space Race) and compile all the files. The software we developed enables members of the crew to track their skills, measured in different ways, while keeping the 5 cognitive domains in mind (Attention, Memory, Visuospatial Skills, Language, and Reasoning & Executive Functions). This software was coded in multiple languages, including JavaScript, CSS and HTML, across the two days. Keeping in mind that this is only a prototype, we visualised and displayed our initial ideas. We incorporated the theme of space and flying a ship with that of cognitive performance, allowing astronauts to track their progress and compete against their crewmates in a friendly competition.

Another software we developed was Vision Lock, which, as the name suggests, is a test for vision. Again, to code this, we used the same three coding languages: JavaScript, CSS and HTML. In order to put this together, we used Visual Studio Code to bring the code to life. The main concept is that, upon starting a session, the crew must adjust the lens in order to focus the image. After a number of attempts, the logs are intended to form a graph displaying visual progression over time, alongside a leaderboard. This makes the process of eye testing more enjoyable for the crew. It is also important to mention that Artificial Intelligence (AI) was used to debug the code.

Another component we developed focuses on hearing health, allowing astronauts to monitor their hearing and simulate the effects of noise exposure in a space environment. Using the Web Audio API, we generated different sound frequencies and adjusted their volume to create a hearing challenge, helping users assess their hearing thresholds. The software also simulates noise exposure during spacecraft activities, such as thruster burns, whilst keeping track of the user's noise dose and considering the effects of wearing earplugs. To develop this feature, we used HTML, JavaScript and Tailwind CSS, working in IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate. We also incorporated Firebase Authentication and Firestore to support individual crew accounts and allow data to synchronise in real time. Additionally, local storage acts as a fallback to ensure that user data can still be saved. Our aim was to make hearing-health monitoring more interactive whilst helping astronauts understand how the noise levels they are exposed to during missions could affect their hearing over time.

We also wanted to incorporate a little comedy into our project, making sure it wasn't all serious and technical. With only 30 seconds to present our video, we decided to make the most of the time limit by speaking like cavemen, keeping our explanations short, simple and straight to the point. We also used a pineapple and an apple as characters to represent health, adding a bit of humour to the message. Playing on the well-known phrase "an apple a day keeps the doctor away", we wanted to show that, in space, an apple a day simply isn't enough! It was a fun way of getting our message across whilst making our project a little more memorable.

Ultimately, we wanted to remind people that before an astronaut is an astronaut, they are human. Behind every spacesuit is a person with a body that gets tired, a mind that needs looking after and a life beyond the mission itself. We can send people millions of miles away, develop incredible technology and explore places we once only imagined, but none of that matters if we forget about the people making it possible. A spacesuit may protect an astronaut from the environment around them, but it cannot protect them from everything their body and mind go through. We wanted the Astrolympics to be a small step towards changing that, because even amongst the stars, human health should never be left behind.
